doc.title: Wycliffe Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Discovering jazz on a great aunt's anthology records
summary: At thirteen he hears a bequeathed five-record jazz anthology in the garage, loves the New Orleans side and Louis Armstrong, and tries to imitate the instruments.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: everything from slave chants up into modern jazz and what they called modern jazz at that time, was up to the Dizzy Gillespie Big Band. And there was “Sonnymoon for Two” by Sonny Rollins, but of everything that I listened to I really loved the side that had the New Orleans jazz on it. I mean it had ragtime, it just had ten different idioms of jazz if you would. And I listened to the “Keyhole Blues,” by Louis Armstrong, and I was in my second, going into my third year playing trombone maybe. And so I began to try to imitate the instruments. And Louis Armstrong sang and I would always just listen to that. At that time we were into the popular music of the day, I think the popular rock group was Kiss, the popular R&B groups were like Rick James or Parliment Funkadellic, Kool and the Gang. So we were into listening to that at the time and I tried to play those things. But when I was by myself I’d always go into the garage and I’d play that record. And so that was pretty much my introduction to jazz. I think my father introduced us to music. But that was my introduction to jazz music.
